answers.answer: DNS resolves api.notes.example, not /notes/42. The stub is the client's local lookup helper; it asks the recursive resolver to obtain an answer. A zone is a managed portion of DNS names; its authoritative servers supply its records. Delegation assigns a child zone to authorities, and referrals point toward them rather than supplying the final host address. With empty caches the recursive resolver asks root, follows its .example referral, then .example's notes.example referral to that authority. It obtains api's CNAME to edge.notes.example and follows that target to usable address data; the data can accompany the alias, otherwise further lookup is needed. CNAME is a name alias, not an address or HTTP redirect. A supplies IPv4; AAAA supplies IPv6; the client uses a reachable family. The resolver returns the result to the stub, then the client connects to an address and sends HTTPS /notes/42 independently of the DNS servers. An address proves neither API health nor ability to serve the note. Later cached addresses or an existing connection may avoid lookup; cached delegations shorten the authority traversal. Alias and target data cache separately, so the alias depends on usable target data.

evidence.quote: DNS, the Domain Name System, provides name discovery. A DNS record is typed data associated with a name. For this web lookup, the client obtains address records, connects to an address, and sends the HTTPS request for /notes/42.

DNS resolves the hostname, not the HTTP path. The later note request and response do not pass through the DNS servers. An address answer does not prove the Notes API is healthy or able to serve that note.
A cache temporarily reuses a stored answer. A usable cached address or an existing connection can avoid a fresh lookup for the next request.

The stub resolver is the client's local lookup helper. It asks a recursive resolver to obtain an answer on its behalf. An authoritative server answers from the records it serves for a zone, a managed portion of DNS names.
Delegation assigns responsibility for a child zone to its authoritative servers. A referral points the resolver toward those servers; it is not the final host address.

Assume empty relevant caches in our teaching hierarchy. The recursive resolver asks root, receives a referral to .example, asks that authority, then follows its referral to the notes.example authority. That authority holds the final records for api.notes.example. Root does not hold every host's address.

The recursive resolver returns the result to the stub. Cached answers can avoid the authority visits; cached delegations can let the resolver start closer to the answer. The stub need not perform each visit itself.

IPv4 and IPv6 are two IP address families. An A record supplies an IPv4 address, such as 192.0.2.10. An AAAA record supplies an IPv6 address, such as 2001:db8::10. A client uses an address family it can reach.

A CNAME record is a name alias. If api.notes.example points to edge.notes.example, resolution follows that target name to obtain its A or AAAA data. The needed data may already be cached or returned with the alias; otherwise further lookup is needed.

The alias contains a DNS name, not an IP address, URL or HTTP path. It does not redirect /notes/42. Without usable target address data, the alias alone cannot give the client an address to connect to.
Alias and target records can be cached separately. The alias adds a dependency on the target's DNS data, even if both names are managed by the same team.

answers.answer: TTL limits ordinary cache reuse in seconds, aged independently by each cache. The resolver received 3600 seconds at 11:59, so its old answer can remain ordinarily usable until 12:59, not necessarily refresh by 12:01. Lowering TTL at noon does not rewrite that entry. For a planned move, lower the TTL before the address switch and allow the previous 3600-second lifetime to age out before switching. Keep the old destination usable through the transition; monitor traffic, errors and existing connections at both destinations to judge when that overlap can end. The lesson gives no fixed universally safe shutdown time: connections do not migrate, independent caches expire differently, and some resolvers can serve expired data when refresh fails. Short TTL increases refresh queries and dependence on functioning DNS, so it cannot guarantee simultaneous worldwide cutover or a hard recovery deadline.

evidence.quote: Now consider a direct address record for api.notes.example instead of the alias. TTL, or time to live, limits ordinary cache reuse in seconds. Each cache ages the TTL it received; it is not a worldwide update timer.

A resolver caches the old address at 10:00 with a 300-second TTL. At 10:01 we change the address and lower TTL to 30 seconds. Its existing entry can still be ordinarily usable until 10:05; the edit does not rewrite that entry.

For a planned move, lower TTL first, allow the previous longer TTL to age out, then switch. Keep the old destination usable through the transition while monitoring traffic, errors and existing connections at both destinations. DNS edits do not migrate open connections.

Shorter TTLs mean more refresh queries and more frequent dependence on working DNS. Independent caches and connection lifetimes prevent a simultaneous cutover. Some resolvers can even serve expired data when refreshing fails, so TTL is not a hard global recovery deadline.

answers.answer: Negative caching reuses an answer reporting absence. The earlier NXDOMAIN says the queried name does not exist, but that cached answer has its own lifetime. Creating the A record does not notify the cache, and its new 30-second positive TTL does not clear the older negative answer. NXDOMAIN concerns name absence. NODATA for AAAA means the name exists without the requested AAAA type; it does not establish absence of A data or of the name. SERVFAIL means resolution could not be completed, perhaps because usable answers could not be obtained; it does not prove nonexistence. Resolution failures can also be cached to avoid repeatedly hammering failing DNS servers. Inspect the queried name, type and status to distinguish these investigations.

evidence.quote: Negative caching reuses an answer reporting absence. NXDOMAIN says the queried name does not exist. NODATA means the name exists but has no record of the requested type: no AAAA record does not imply no A record or no name.

Suppose a resolver cached NXDOMAIN before we created api.notes.example. Adding its A record does not notify that cache. The negative answer has its own cache lifetime; the new positive record's TTL does not clear it.

SERVFAIL means resolution could not be completed, for example because the resolver could not obtain usable answers. It is not proof that the name does not exist. Resolution failures may also be cached to avoid repeatedly hammering failing DNS servers.
Check the requested name, record type and returned status before changing records. A missing type, a cached absent name and a lookup failure call for different investigations.

answers.answer: Steering selects destinations returned in DNS answers; failover changes the selected destination after failure. A separate health check with policy, or an operator, must detect east's failure and change the answers; ordinary records do not detect application health. Equal lookup answers do not mean equal HTTP request counts: a shared resolver reuses one answer for many clients, and a client can send many requests through one address or connection. Removing east only changes new answers; clients with cached east data can still try it, and open connections do not migrate. DNS does not select again for every HTTP request. West must be reachable and healthy with enough spare capacity for the redirected work. Health checks sample behavior and cannot promise every request succeeds; changing DNS neither creates capacity nor guarantees immediate recovery.

evidence.quote: DNS traffic steering selects destinations returned in answers. Failover changes the selected destination after failure. For Notes east and west, a separate health check and policy, or an operator, must detect east's failure and change answers. Ordinary DNS records do not detect application health themselves.

Returning east for half of lookups does not guarantee half of HTTP requests reach east. A shared recursive resolver can reuse one answer for many clients, and each client may send many requests using that address or connection.

After east is removed from new answers, cached clients can still try it. Existing connections do not migrate to west just because DNS changed. DNS is not choosing a destination again for every HTTP request.

West must be reachable, healthy and have enough spare capacity for redirected work. A health signal is a sample, not a promise that every request succeeds; DNS changes do not create capacity or guarantee instant recovery.

answers.answer: An open connection can keep working without lookup, and a usable cached address may allow a new connection even during a DNS outage. New uncached users need reachable recursive resolution, correct delegation and answering authorities, so their failures can coexist with working sessions. Inspect the client's recursive resolver first: queried name and type, answer/error and remaining TTL. Compare authoritative data and parent delegation for wrong or failed results. A new authoritative address alongside an old cached one suggests cache age rather than automatically requiring another edit. Once the expected address is obtained, investigate connection, HTTPS and application outcomes separately. An HTTP 500 shows an HTTP service responded with an error, not by itself a DNS lookup failure; successful discovery cannot establish application health. Reachable alternate resolvers and authoritative servers reduce individual server failures, but cannot correct a shared wrong record, broken delegation or failed Notes API; duplicate bad configuration can return the same wrong result.

evidence.quote: During a DNS outage, a client with a usable cached address may still connect, and an open connection may keep working without a lookup. Fresh uncached lookups need a reachable recursive resolver, working delegation and authoritative servers that can answer.

Reachable alternate resolvers and authoritative servers reduce individual server failures. They cannot fix a shared wrong record, broken delegation or a failed Notes API. Several DNS servers with the same bad configuration can return the same wrong result.

Start with the client's recursive resolver: inspect the queried name and type, its answer or error, and remaining TTL. Compare authoritative data and parent delegation when results are wrong or failing. An authoritative new address beside a cached old one suggests a cache-age question, not an automatic need for another edit.

Once the expected address is obtained, inspect connection, HTTPS and application results separately. HTTP 500 means an HTTP service responded with an error; it is not by itself a DNS lookup failure. Successful DNS does not prove the application works.

answers.answer: DNSSEC signs DNS data. A validating resolver checks signatures through a chain of trust starting at a configured trusted key, with each trusted signing key vouching for the next link. Successful validation establishes the signed data's origin and integrity, detecting alteration. It does not encrypt or hide the query, certify Notes health or guarantee availability. It does not remove HTTPS certificate validation. HTTPS separately authenticates the endpoint by certificate validation and encrypts the HTTP exchange. The client must verify api.notes.example, the requested hostname, even if DNS resolves via edge.notes.example. DNS validation also grants no permission to read notes; application access rules remain.

evidence.quote: DNSSEC adds signatures to DNS data. A validating resolver checks those signatures through a chain of trust: each trusted signing key vouches for the next link, starting at a configured trusted key. Successful validation establishes the signed data's origin and integrity, meaning it has not been altered without detection.

That validates DNS data, not the Notes application. DNSSEC does not encrypt the query, certify service health or guarantee availability. Unsigned data does not gain these signature checks merely because a resolver supports DNSSEC.

HTTPS separately authenticates the endpoint through certificate validation and encrypts the HTTP exchange. The client must still verify the certificate for the hostname it requested, api.notes.example, even if DNS followed an alias to edge.notes.example.
A valid DNSSEC answer does not remove HTTPS certificate checks. Nor does discovering a real server give the caller permission to read every note; the application's access rules still apply.
